title: Revenue dropped 20%: which queries first?
prompt: Yesterday's revenue on an e-commerce dashboard is 20% lower than the same day last week. You have tables orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, city, payment_mode) and order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price). Explain, step by step, which SQL checks you would run and what each one tells you.

rubric.point: First checks data correctness (pipeline delay, missing/duplicate rows, status changes) before assuming a business drop
Breaks revenue into orders × AOV (or similar decomposition) to locate the driver
Slices by meaningful dimensions (city, payment mode, category, new vs returning, status/cancellations)
Mentions concrete SQL constructs (GROUP BY date/city, comparing with last week, conditional aggregation)
Clear, structured communication of findings / next step

model: First rule out a data problem: compare today's row counts and max(order_date) with normal days, and check for duplicates or a delayed load. Next, split revenue = number of orders × average order value, grouping by date for both days, to see which part fell. Then slice the drop: GROUP BY city, payment_mode, product category and status. A spike in cancellations, one city going to zero (an outage) or one payment mode failing (a UPI gateway issue) usually explains it. Finally, compare new vs returning customers. Report the biggest contributor with numbers and suggest the owner to contact.

title: Why does this report double count?
prompt: An analyst joins customers (1 row per customer) to orders (many per customer) and to support_tickets (many per customer) in one query, then does SUM(orders.amount) per customer. The totals are much higher than finance's numbers. Explain why, and how you would fix it.

rubric.point: Identifies fan-out / row multiplication from joining two one-to-many tables (orders × tickets)
Gives a small numeric example of the multiplication
Fix: aggregate each child table to customer level first (CTEs/subqueries) then join, or use separate queries
Mentions validating against a known total / COUNT(DISTINCT)

model: Joining customers to two one-to-many tables multiplies rows: a customer with 3 orders and 2 tickets produces 3 × 2 = 6 rows, so every order amount is counted twice. The fix is to aggregate each child table to customer level first, e.g. WITH o AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id), t AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS tickets FROM support_tickets GROUP BY customer_id), then join both to customers. Always reconcile the grand total against a trusted number after changing joins.

title: WHERE vs HAVING in your own words
prompt: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING to a junior teammate, with one example query where using the wrong one would give a wrong or failing result.

rubric.point: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
Mentions logical order of execution (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT)
Gives a correct example (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5, WHERE status='delivered')
Clear, simple language

model: WHERE works on individual rows before any grouping, so it can't use aggregates. HAVING works on groups after GROUP BY, so it can. The logical order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Example: to find customers with more than 5 delivered orders, write SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5. Writing WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 fails, and putting status = 'delivered' in HAVING is invalid because status isn't grouped.

title: Choose: RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER?
prompt: For each case, say which ranking function you'd use and why: (a) show exactly one latest order per customer; (b) find the 2nd highest distinct salary; (c) a leaderboard where tied students share a position and the next position is skipped.

rubric.point: (a) ROW_NUMBER with correct partition/order and filtering rn = 1
(b) DENSE_RANK = 2 (or explains why RANK may skip)
(c) RANK, with explanation of gaps after ties
Explanation of tie behaviour with a tiny example

model: (a) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC), keeping rn = 1. It always returns exactly one row per customer, even on ties. (b) DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 2, because DENSE_RANK has no gaps, so the 2nd distinct value always gets rank 2. (c) RANK(): ties share a position and the next one is skipped. For salaries 100, 100, 90: ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3, RANK gives 1,1,3 and DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2.

title: Make a slow query faster
prompt: A daily report query takes 4 minutes: SELECT * FROM events WHERE YEAR(event_time) = 2025 AND LOWER(city) = 'pune' ORDER BY event_time. The table has 200 million rows. Suggest improvements and explain why each helps.

rubric.point: Avoid functions on filtered columns (use event_time range; store/compare normalized city) so indexes can be used (sargability)
Select only needed columns instead of SELECT *
Appropriate index (e.g. composite on city, event_time) and/or partitioning by date
Mentions checking EXPLAIN / execution plan
Mentions limiting/aggregating results or precomputing for a daily report

model: Wrapping columns in functions (YEAR(), LOWER()) stops the database from using indexes. Rewrite the filter as event_time >= '2025-01-01' AND event_time < '2026-01-01' AND city = 'Pune' (store city in a consistent case). Replace SELECT * with only the columns the report needs. Add a composite index on (city, event_time), or partition the table by date so only 2025 partitions are scanned. Check EXPLAIN before and after. For a daily report, consider a pre-aggregated summary table refreshed each night.

title: Explain NULL traps
prompt: Give two situations where NULL values can silently produce wrong results in SQL, and how you would guard against each.

rubric.point: Correct trap 1 (e.g. = NULL never true / NOT IN with NULL returns nothing)
Correct trap 2 (e.g. AVG/COUNT(col) ignore NULLs, SUM returns NULL, arithmetic with NULL)
Correct guards (IS NULL, COALESCE, NOT EXISTS, explicit business rule)
Clarity / example

model: 1) x NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees) returns no rows if any dept_id is NULL, because the comparison becomes unknown. Use NOT EXISTS instead. 2) Aggregates skip NULLs: AVG(salary) ignores missing salaries, and COUNT(salary) counts fewer rows than COUNT(*), so averages can look higher than expected. Decide the business rule and use COALESCE(salary, 0) only if missing really means zero. Also, = NULL is never true, so always use IS NULL.

title: Normalization with an example
prompt: Take this table: student_courses(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_name, instructor, instructor_phone). Explain which problems it has, and normalise it step by step to 3NF.

rubric.point: Identifies anomalies (update/insert/delete) caused by redundancy
Correct key and partial dependency → 2NF split (students, courses, enrollment)
Transitive dependency (instructor → phone) → 3NF split
Final tables with keys stated

model: Problems: student and course details repeat on every row, so changing an instructor's phone means updating many rows (update anomaly). A course can't exist without a student (insert anomaly), and removing the last student deletes the course (delete anomaly). The key is (student_id, course_id). student_name depends only on student_id, and course details depend only on course_id, which are partial dependencies. Split into students(student_id, student_name), courses(course_id, course_name, instructor) and enrollments(student_id, course_id) for 2NF. instructor_phone depends on instructor, not on the course key (transitive), so move it to instructors(instructor, instructor_phone) for 3NF.

title: ACID with a UPI example
prompt: Explain each ACID property using a UPI money transfer of ₹500 from A to B.

rubric.point: Atomicity: debit and credit both happen or neither
Consistency: rules/constraints hold (no negative balance, total money preserved)
Isolation: concurrent transfers don't see partial states / interfere
Durability: once committed, survives crashes

model: Atomicity: the ₹500 debit from A and credit to B happen together or not at all. If the credit fails, the debit is rolled back. Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another (A can't go below zero, and the total money in the system stays the same). Isolation: if A sends money to two people at the same moment, each transaction behaves as if it ran alone, so one can't read A's half-updated balance. Durability: once the app shows 'success' (committed), the transfer survives even if the bank's server crashes a second later.

title: When would you NOT add an index?
prompt: Indexes make reads faster. Explain how an index helps, and give at least three situations where adding an index is a bad idea.

rubric.point: Explains index as sorted structure (B-tree) enabling lookup without full scan
Write overhead (inserts/updates slower)
Low-cardinality columns / small tables gain little
Storage cost and/or columns rarely filtered, or queries using functions/leading wildcards
Clarity

model: An index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree, like the index at the back of a book. The database can jump straight to the matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. Avoid indexes when: (1) the table is write-heavy, because every insert or update must also update each index; (2) the column has very few distinct values (status with 3 values over millions of rows), so the index barely narrows the search; (3) the table is tiny, where a full scan is already fast; (4) the column is rarely used in WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY. Indexes also take disk space.

title: Primary key vs unique vs foreign key
prompt: Explain the differences between a primary key, a unique constraint and a foreign key, using an orders and customers example.

rubric.point: Primary key: unique + not null, one per table, identifies row
Unique: no duplicates, can allow NULL, many per table (e.g. email)
Foreign key: references parent PK, enforces referential integrity (orders.customer_id)
Example clarity

model: customers.customer_id is the primary key: unique, never NULL, and only one per table. It identifies each customer. customers.email can have a UNIQUE constraint: no two customers share an email, but it may allow NULL, and a table can have several unique constraints. orders.customer_id is a foreign key that references customers.customer_id: the database refuses an order for a customer who doesn't exist, which keeps referential integrity.

title: OLTP vs OLAP for a food-delivery company
prompt: A food-delivery company runs its app on MySQL and wants dashboards on 3 years of orders. Explain why analysts shouldn't run heavy reports on the app database, and what you'd set up instead.

rubric.point: OLTP characteristics (many small transactions, normalised, latency-sensitive)
Risk: heavy analytical scans slow down/lock the live app
OLAP/warehouse characteristics (columnar, denormalised star schema, history)
Pipeline: replicate/ETL into warehouse, BI on top
Clarity

model: The MySQL app database is OLTP: thousands of small, fast inserts and updates (orders, rider status) on a normalised schema, where every millisecond matters to customers. A 3-year aggregation scans millions of rows and can slow down or lock the live app. Instead, copy data nightly or incrementally (or via CDC) into an OLAP warehouse like BigQuery, Snowflake or Redshift. Warehouses are columnar and built for big scans, and you model the data as a star schema (fact_orders with dim_restaurant, dim_date and so on) for Power BI or Tableau.

title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
prompt: Compare DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. When would you use each? Can each be rolled back?

rubric.point: DELETE: removes selected rows with WHERE, DML, logged, can be rolled back in a transaction
TRUNCATE: removes all rows fast, keeps structure, DDL in most DBs, limited rollback
DROP: removes the table structure and data
Appropriate use cases

model: DELETE removes chosen rows (WHERE), logs each row, fires triggers and can be rolled back inside a transaction. Use it to remove specific records. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly and keeps the table structure. It's DDL in most databases, is minimally logged, often resets identity counters, and usually can't be rolled back (it can in PostgreSQL inside a transaction). Use it to empty a staging table. DROP deletes the table itself, structure and data. Use it when the table is no longer needed.

title: Orders dropped in one city
prompt: A food-delivery app's orders in Pune fell 30% this week while other cities are stable. How would you find the root cause? Mention the metrics and data you'd look at.

rubric.point: Validates data first (tracking/pipeline issue, definition change)
Funnel breakdown: app opens → restaurant views → cart → checkout → payment success
Internal causes: supply (restaurants/riders), pricing/fees, app release, payments
External causes: weather, festivals, competitor offers, local events
Structured approach and prioritised next step

model: 1) Confirm the data: is Pune tracking or the pipeline broken? Did an order definition change? 2) Locate the drop in the funnel: app opens, restaurant page views, add to cart, checkout and payment success, compared with last week. 3) If demand (opens) is flat but conversion fell, check supply (fewer restaurants online, rider shortage, longer delivery times), price changes (delivery fee, surge), a new app release, or payment failures. 4) If opens fell, check external factors: heavy rain, a festival, a competitor discount, a local strike. Slice by area, cuisine and new vs repeat users, quantify each factor, and share the top cause with owners.

title: Which metrics for a new feature?
prompt: An e-commerce app launches a 'Buy Now, Pay Later' option at checkout. Which metrics would you track to judge whether it's working? Include at least one guardrail metric.

rubric.point: Primary success metric tied to goal (checkout conversion / orders / GMV)
Adoption metrics (% of orders using BNPL, by segment)
Guardrails (default/repayment rate, returns/cancellations, cost, cannibalisation of other payment modes)
Mentions comparison method (A/B test or before–after with control)
Clarity

model: Goal: more completed purchases. Primary metric: checkout conversion rate and orders per user (or GMV) for users offered BNPL vs not, ideally through an A/B test. Adoption: share of orders paid with BNPL, split by new vs repeat users and by order value. Guardrails: BNPL default or late-repayment rate, return and cancellation rate for BNPL orders, payment-partner cost per order, and whether BNPL just moved users away from UPI or cards without adding orders. Success means conversion rises while the guardrails stay within agreed limits.

title: Guesstimate: daily UPI transactions at a college canteen
prompt: Estimate the number of UPI transactions per day at a college canteen with about 3,000 students. Show your assumptions clearly.

rubric.point: Clear structure (population → visitors → transactions per visitor → UPI share)
Reasonable, stated assumptions
Correct arithmetic
Sanity check or range

model: Students: 3,000; about 80% on campus on a weekday gives 2,400. Say 60% visit the canteen, which is about 1,440 visitors. Each visitor makes about 1.5 purchases (tea, snacks, lunch), giving about 2,160 purchases. Add staff, about 200 purchases, for roughly 2,360. If around 75% are paid by UPI, that's about 1,770 UPI transactions a day. Sanity check: over a 10-hour day, that's about 3 per minute, which is plausible at busy times. Range: 1,200–2,500 depending on attendance and the UPI share.

title: Interpret an A/B test result
prompt: A test of a new onboarding screen shows conversion 12.0% (treatment) vs 10.0% (control), with 2,000 users in each group. The product manager wants to launch tomorrow. What would you check before agreeing?

rubric.point: Statistical significance / confidence interval (and roughly whether 2k each is enough)
Sample ratio / randomisation checks and test duration (weekday effects, novelty)
Guardrail metrics (retention, revenue, support tickets)
Segment consistency and practical significance (is +2pp worth it)
Clear recommendation

model: Check that the difference is statistically significant: with 2,000 users per group, a 2-point lift gives a z-score of roughly 2, which is borderline, so look at the confidence interval. Confirm the split really was random and close to 50/50 (sample ratio mismatch), and that the test ran for at least a full week to cover weekday patterns and novelty effects. Look at guardrails such as day-7 retention, revenue per user and support tickets, and whether the lift holds across platforms and new vs returning users. If it's significant and the guardrails are fine, launch, perhaps with a gradual rollout. Otherwise, extend the test.

title: Increase repeat purchases
prompt: An online fashion store's repeat purchase rate is 18%. Using data, how would you find ways to increase it? What analysis would you do first?

rubric.point: Defines the metric precisely (window, delivered orders)
Segments customers (cohort, category, acquisition channel, first-order experience like returns/delivery delay)
Finds drivers by comparing repeaters vs non-repeaters
Proposes testable actions (personalised offers, timing based on inter-purchase gap) with measurement
Clarity

model: First define it: the share of customers with a second delivered order within 90 days of their first. Compare repeaters with one-time buyers on their first-order experience (delivery time, returns, discount used), first category, acquisition channel and city, using cohorts by first-order month. Find the typical gap between first and second orders. Patterns like 'customers whose first order was late rarely return' or 'Instagram-acquired users repeat less' point to fixes. Then test actions: a reminder or offer timed around the usual reorder gap, better delivery promises, and recommendations based on the first category. Measure each with a holdout group.

title: Explain a dashboard number to a non-technical manager
prompt: Your dashboard shows 'Average delivery time: 42 minutes', but the operations manager says most orders arrive in about 30 minutes. How would you investigate and explain the difference simply?

rubric.point: Recognises mean vs median / skew from outliers
Checks definition (start/end timestamps, cancelled orders, time zones)
Suggests better metric (median, P90, % within SLA)
Simple, non-technical explanation

model: Two likely reasons. First, an average is pulled up by a few very late orders: if most orders take 30 minutes but some take 2 hours, the mean can be 42 while the median is 30. Second, check the definition: does the clock start at order time or at restaurant acceptance? Are cancelled or rescheduled orders included? Are there time-zone issues? To the manager: 'A typical order does take 30 minutes. The 42 is pulled up by a small number of very late deliveries.' Then show the median, the 90th percentile and '% delivered within 35 minutes', which describe the experience better.

title: Batch or streaming?
prompt: For each, say batch or streaming and why: (a) monthly sales report for leadership; (b) blocking suspicious card transactions; (c) live order-tracking map for customers; (d) training a recommendation model weekly.

rubric.point: (a) batch with reason
(b) streaming with reason (low-latency decision)
(c) streaming / near real-time with reason
(d) batch with reason
Mentions cost/complexity trade-off

model: (a) Batch: leadership looks at it monthly, so nightly or monthly jobs are cheaper and simpler. (b) Streaming: the decision has to happen within seconds, before the payment completes. (c) Streaming or near real-time: customers expect the rider's location to update every few seconds. (d) Batch: weekly retraining on historical data doesn't need real-time input. Streaming adds cost and complexity, so use it only when low latency creates real value.

title: Design a daily orders pipeline
prompt: Design a pipeline that takes orders from the app's MySQL database and makes a daily sales dashboard available by 8 AM. Describe the steps, tools and how you'd handle failures.

rubric.point: Ingestion approach (incremental/CDC, to lake or staging)
Transformation and modelling (clean, dedupe, fact/dimension or aggregates)
Orchestration and scheduling (e.g. Airflow DAG with dependencies)
Data quality checks and failure handling (retries, alerts, idempotent loads)
Clear end-to-end flow

model: At 5 AM an Airflow DAG starts: (1) extract yesterday's new or changed orders from MySQL incrementally on updated_at (or via CDC) and land them as Parquet in S3 or ADLS (raw layer); (2) clean and deduplicate with Spark or dbt, and join products and customers (silver); (3) MERGE into fact_orders and build daily_sales aggregates in the warehouse (gold); (4) run tests: unique order_id, not-null keys, revenue within an expected range of the last 4 same weekdays; (5) refresh the BI dataset. Tasks retry with backoff, and loads are idempotent (MERGE or partition overwrite), so reruns are safe. Failures alert the team before 8 AM.

title: Why is my Spark job slow?
prompt: A PySpark job joining a 500-million-row transactions table with a 2,000-row merchants table takes 2 hours, and the Spark UI shows one task running far longer than the others. What is likely happening and how would you fix it?

rubric.point: Identifies data skew (one key with huge volume) from the straggler task
Broadcast join for the small merchants table to avoid shuffling the big table
Other fixes: salting, AQE skew join, filtering/selecting early, proper partitions
Mentions verifying with Spark UI / plan

model: One very slow task usually means data skew: a few merchant_ids (a big marketplace, say) hold a large share of the transactions, so the task handling that key does most of the work. Since merchants has only 2,000 rows, broadcast it (broadcast(merchants)) so the 500M-row table doesn't need to shuffle at all. That alone often fixes it. Other options: enable Adaptive Query Execution's skew-join handling, salt the hot keys, and filter rows and select only needed columns before the join. Confirm the improvement in the Spark UI (shuffle size, task time spread).

title: ETL vs ELT for a startup
prompt: A startup is moving its reporting to BigQuery. Should it use ETL or ELT? Explain the difference and recommend one, with reasons and one risk to manage.

rubric.point: Correct difference (where transform happens)
Recommends ELT for cloud warehouse with sound reasons (elastic compute, raw history, SQL/dbt)
Notes when ETL is better (PII masking / pre-load filtering)
Names a risk and mitigation (cost control, governance, raw data access)

model: ETL transforms data on a separate system before loading. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse. For a startup on BigQuery, ELT fits: compute is elastic, raw history is kept so logic can be re-run, and transformations become version-controlled SQL (dbt) that analysts can also maintain. Use an ETL-style step where sensitive fields (phone, PAN) must be masked before loading. Risks: query costs can grow and raw tables can be misused. Manage this with partitioned tables, cost alerts and access control on raw datasets.

title: Track customer address changes (SCD)
prompt: In a sales warehouse, customers sometimes move cities. The business wants old sales to stay under the city where they happened. How would you model the customer dimension? Explain with an example.

rubric.point: Chooses SCD Type 2 and explains why (history needed)
Describes columns: surrogate key, valid_from/valid_to, is_current
Explains how facts link to the correct version (surrogate key at load time)
Worked example (Pune → Bengaluru)

model: Use SCD Type 2. dim_customer has a surrogate key (customer_sk), the business key (customer_id), attributes like city, and valid_from, valid_to and is_current. When Riya moves from Pune to Bengaluru on 1 July, the Pune row gets valid_to = 30 June and is_current = 0, and a new row (new customer_sk) is inserted with city = Bengaluru, valid_from = 1 July and is_current = 1. Each fact row stores the customer_sk that was current when the sale happened, so June sales stay under Pune and July sales go to Bengaluru.

title: Data lake turning into a swamp
prompt: A company dumped years of raw files into a data lake. Now nobody trusts or finds anything, and queries are slow. Suggest practical improvements.

rubric.point: Organise into layers (bronze/silver/gold or raw/clean/curated)
Catalogue/metadata, ownership and documentation
Quality checks and table formats with ACID/schema (Delta/Iceberg)
Performance: columnar formats, partitioning, compaction of small files
Prioritisation / clarity

model: 1) Organise it: keep raw data in a bronze zone, build cleaned and deduplicated silver tables, and business-ready gold tables for reporting. 2) Make it findable: add a data catalogue (Glue, Unity Catalog, Purview) with owners, descriptions and freshness. 3) Make it trustworthy: use Delta or Iceberg tables for ACID writes and schema enforcement, plus automated quality checks. 4) Make it fast: convert CSV and JSON to Parquet, partition by commonly filtered columns like date, and compact small files. Start with the 5–10 datasets people use most.
